analysis.one_liner: Extends expiring Affordable Care Act premium subsidies for two years and raises the income cap to six times poverty.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to extend and reshape the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, introduced with 12 cosponsors from both parties, has sat in two House committees with no hearing or vote since November 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The enhanced premium tax credits that have lowered health insurance premiums for people buying coverage on their own are scheduled to run out. This bill keeps that enhanced subsidy structure in place for 2026 and 2027 and raises the income ceiling for help from four times the poverty line to six times, so middle-income households keep getting aid. It also tightens Medicare Advantage payment rules so plans get paid based on two years of patient data and can't boost payments from diagnoses gathered in chart reviews or health questionnaires, and it cracks down on insurance brokers who enroll people in plans without their knowledge, adding civil and criminal penalties and new verification rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy their own health insurance through the ACA marketplaces, especially the millions above four times the poverty line who would otherwise lose subsidy help entirely when the enhanced credits expire, and lower-income enrollees who would see premiums jump. Patients also benefit from less fraud in broker-driven enrollment and Medicare dollars no longer inflated by extra diagnoses recorded on paper.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the enhanced premium tax credit table through 2027 and raises the subsidy income cap from 400% to 600% of the poverty line, so households well into middle-income territory keep premium help [S2].

Requires Medicare Advantage plans' payments to be based on two years of diagnostic data, excludes diagnoses collected from chart reviews and health risk assessments, and directs the government to adjust payments for plans' more aggressive coding patterns — reducing payments that grow when plans record more diagnoses [S2].

Imposes civil penalties of $10,000 to $50,000 per affected person for negligent broker violations, up to $200,000 for knowing fraud, and criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison, plus a verification process requiring documented consumer consent before broker-assisted enrollments take effect [S2].

Requires consumers to be notified of any enrollment or agent-of-record changes with plain-language instructions for canceling unauthorized activity, and delays broker commissions until inconsistencies in an application are resolved [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the cost of extending the subsidies (the bill contains no offsetting spending cuts or tax increases). Medicare Advantage insurers also bear reduced payments under the tighter risk-adjustment rules, and brokers and marketing firms face new penalties, audits, and commission delays.

drawbacks.text: The two-year extension is deficit-financed: the bill includes no offsets, so extending subsidies to households up to 600% of the poverty line — roughly $150,000 for a family of four — adds to federal spending, and critics note some of that aid goes to families who could afford coverage on their own.
The extension is temporary and does nothing about the underlying premiums, which have risen sharply; after 2027 the same affordability cliff returns unless Congress acts again.

The Medicare Advantage and broker-fraud provisions trade speed for rigor: requiring two years of diagnostic data and excluding chart-review diagnoses lowers plan payments, which insurers argue could squeeze benefits, though the bill directs the process to preserve continuity of coverage for enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — keeping premiums affordable for people who buy their own insurance and the aid reaching further up the income scale — is a large, direct benefit to millions of households, and the fraud and payment-integrity provisions plausibly recover some of the cost. The honest objections are that it is a two-year patch financed entirely by borrowing, and that it extends help well up the income scale. On balance the benefits to enrollees are large and concrete; the fiscal cost is real and left unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 10, 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has sat with no hearing or vote as the end of 2025 approaches and the enhanced credits near expiration.

narrative.text: Representative Sam Liccardo (D-CA) introduced the bill on November 10, 2025, joined as original cosponsors by Representatives Kiley (R-CA), Bacon (R-NE), Goodlander (D-NH), and Ross (D-NC) [S2].
The bill has 12 cosponsors, split 7 Republicans and 5 Democrats [S3].
It was referred to both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day of introduction; the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote since [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has acted, which favors the industries the bill would constrain: marketplace insurers keep subsidy-driven customers without the new broker-fraud verification rules, Medicare Advantage plans avoid the tighter coding-based payment rules, and brokers avoid the new penalties — while marketplace enrollees face sharply higher premiums if the credits lapse on schedule.

for.name: Rep. Sam Liccardo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill extending and modifying the enhanced premium tax credit, paired with Medicare Advantage payment-integrity and broker-fraud provisions.

for.name: Rep. Kevin Kiley
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill Republican sponsorship from day one.

for.name: Reps. Debbie Dingell-aligned cosponsors: Goodlander and Ross
for.what_they_did: Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) and Deborah Ross (D-NC) joined as original cosponsors.

against.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled this bill for a floor vote; during the November 2025 funding fight he declined to commit to extending the enhanced subsidies, and the House instead moved on its own narrower approach.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely bipartisan — 7 of the bill's 12 cosponsors are Republicans and 5 are Democrats — but no vote has been scheduled, so the partisan test hasn't happened yet.

industries.note: The bill keeps federal premium subsidies flowing through private ACA plans and extends that support to households up to 600% of poverty, locking in insurers' role as the paid channel for affordability aid. It also subjects their enrollment chain to new verification, audit, and marketing rules, and delays broker commissions until applications are clean.

The bill requires payment calculations to use two years of diagnostic data, excludes diagnoses gathered through chart reviews and health risk assessments, and directs the government to fully adjust for plans' more aggressive coding patterns — reducing payments that currently grow whenever a plan records more diagnoses. The savings run to Medicare and taxpayers rather than to the plans.

industries.industry: Health insurance agents, brokers, and marketing firms
industries.note: The bill creates civil penalties of up to $200,000 per person for knowing fraud and up to 10 years in prison for willful false enrollment information, requires documented consumer consent and audits, and pays commissions only after inconsistencies are resolved. Legitimate agents keep working under tighter rules; fraudulent enrollment pipelines are the target.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is barely two weeks old and sits before two committees with no scheduled action, while the enhanced credits it would extend are set to lapse at the end of 2025 and open-enrollment premiums are already reflecting that. Congress is instead working on rival, narrower proposals, so unless House leadership picks up this bipartisan framework directly, the likely path is the same one most subsidy-extension bills take: committee referral with no vote before the credits expire, possibly revisited retroactively later.
